title: The impact understanding of exosome therapy in COVID-19 and preparations for the future approaches in dealing with infec

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 4 is titled 'Comparing cytokine levels after exosome treatment using paired T-test' and the footnote states 'SD, Standard deviation; 95% CI, 95% Confidence interval; t, test statistic, Cohen’s d', but the actual columns report 'Median ± IQR', 'Z', 'P-value', and 'r', and the footnote also refers to Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test. The table is not a paired t-test and does not present the declared t/Cohen's d/SD/CI statistics.

Table 4 reports P = 0.043 with Z = -2.023 for paired comparisons with n = 5. For an exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test with n = 5 and no ties, the smallest possible p-value is 0.0625, so P = 0.043 is not an exact p-value for n = 5. Reporting an asymptotic p-value with such a small sample is inappropriate and inconsistent with the stated nonparametric test.

Table 4 reports Z = -2.023 and r = 0.64, while the footnote says r is calculated via Z/√N and n = 5. With n = 5, |r| = 2.023/√5 ≈ 0.905, not 0.64. The value 0.64 corresponds approximately to N = 10, contradicting the stated sample size and formula.

The text states that doses of 10, 20, 40, and 60 µg/mL were evaluated, but then says 'a dose of 40 µg/mL (the highest dose) was selected as the optimal dose'. Since 60 µg/mL was also tested, 40 µg/mL cannot be described as the highest dose.

The abstract says the five COVID-19 patients 'were subjected to both inactivated SARS-CoV-2 and exosome therapy' and the conclusion states 'exosome administration can effectively mitigate the hyperinflammation induced by COVID-19'. The experiments were performed on isolated PBMCs in vitro, not by administering exosomes to patients. This language overstates the clinical evidence and implies in vivo therapy that was not performed.
